what_it_does: Designing a computer chip involves routing millions of wires through a dense grid — a step called maze routing, where algorithms find paths for each wire while avoiding obstacles and other wires. Doing this on a GPU (a processor with thousands of small cores that run things in parallel) is appealing because it could dramatically speed up the process, but two problems arise at large chip scales: the routing data structures exceed the GPU's on-chip memory, and the common sweep-based approach (which processes the routing grid in directional passes) launches an enormous number of small GPU tasks, adding significant overhead. This paper introduces a technique called sweep-sharing, where multiple wires are routed simultaneously within a single sweep pass rather than one at a time, which cuts both memory use and the number of task launches. It also adds an edge-level repair strategy that, when a wire segment causes a conflict, only re-routes the conflicting segment rather than the entire wire path, saving time. Together these techniques are claimed to make GPU-accelerated maze routing scalable to large, industrial chip designs.
